Bounded, and refused (never truncated) past the bound: a full-text condition is at most 512 characters and 64 words, a substring needle (from/to/cc/header) at most 50 bytes as a LIKE pattern, the tree at most 32 levels deep and 512 nodes, and at most 64 bound values in total (an inMailboxOtherThan element costs one each).

info.description: Message store + routing core: mailbox Durable Objects, R2 blobs, D1 directory. Every route requires a bearer credential (401 unauthorized without one) except four: GET /api/v1/health; GET /api/v1/pim/feeds/{token} and GET /api/v1/deliveries/fetch/{token}, where the token in the path IS the credential (a calendar feed, and a webhook's fetch capability for an attachment or the raw message); and GET /api/v1/branding/*, the public white-label reads a login screen needs before any credential exists (which answer a uniform 404 for an unknown domain and an unbranded one alike). Mailbox-scoped app passwords are refused on directory routes with 403 insufficient_scope. Errors always answer { error: "snake_case_code", ... } — schema failures as { error: "validation_failed", issues }.

post.description:
**The SMTP-shaped route: for submission agents, not applications.** One recipient per call — you fan out and collect a verdict per RCPT, mirroring an SMTP transaction. Application code almost always wants `POST /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/send`, which takes JSON, builds the MIME, and returns every recipient's result from one call.

**Response codes are durable guarantees.** `200 delivered` comes only after the full two-phase commit; `202 queued` only once the blob is durably staged and a queue job exists. For an MTA the mapping is `4xx` = permanent failure (bounce), `5xx` = retry with the same `X-Delivery-Id` — the retry converges, because everything in the delivery path is idempotent.

Every RFC 5322 `From:` address must ladder-resolve to the sending mailbox on a domain that may send (`invalid_from` / `from_not_owned` / `from_sending_disabled`), which is what keeps the outbound DKIM signature DMARC-aligned.

Two representations of the same resource. Without an `Accept: application/json` header you get the stored bytes verbatim — what a DAV client needs. With it you get a JSContact Card (RFC 9553), which is what a browser client wants: no vCard parser in the page, and unmapped properties preserved through a read-modify-write by the escape hatches.

`data` is null when the stored body has no JSON mapping — a body that does not parse — and `content` carries the wire text in that case. `writable` is false when the object converts to JSON but could not be converted back — it is display-only.

The one call behind a mail client's Accept / Tentative / Decline buttons. Name the invitation — either `messageId` (+ the `section` from `…/messages/{id}/invitation`, or omit it and let the server pick the scheduling part) or the raw `ics` inline — and give a PARTSTAT; it files an attendee copy into the default calendar if the event is not already stored, then records the reply and tells the organizer — patching their copy in place when they are local, mailing them a `METHOD:REPLY` when they are not.

This endpoint refuses exactly that — the caller must be an ATTENDEE and must not be the ORGANIZER — and the filing it performs is an attendee copy, which never schedules.

Two representations of the same resource. Without an `Accept: application/json` header you get the stored bytes verbatim — what a DAV client needs. With it you get a JSCalendar Event or Task (RFC 8984 — a VEVENT reads as an Event, a VTODO as a Task, and `@type` says which), which is what a browser client wants: no iCalendar parser in the page, and unmapped properties preserved through a read-modify-write by the escape hatches.

get.description:
Upgrades to a WebSocket that streams best-effort change signals for this mailbox: message.new (delivery), message.updated / message.expunged / message.restored / message.purged, label.expunged (IMAP EXPUNGE), label.created / label.renamed / label.deleted, trash.emptied, thread.merged (an arrival joined two conversations — re-list thread views, since thread ids are convergent rather than stable), and state.changed. Each frame is `{ v, type, ts, data }` with identifiers only — never message content. The vocabulary is additive: treat an unrecognized `type` as a generic 'something changed' nudge rather than an error.

Signals are not a journal: there is no replay or backlog, so on every (re)connect re-sync and treat each event as 'this changed, re-fetch it'. A `state.changed` frame carries the current state token for each type (`{ Email, Mailbox, Thread, EmailDelivery }`); its `Email` value is exactly what `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages/changes` accepts as `since`, so a client can re-sync incrementally instead of re-listing. A `ready` frame with the session deadline is sent on connect; the session is closed with code 4401 (session_expired — reconnect with a fresh bearer) after 12h, 4403 (credential_revoked — the app password was revoked; do not reconnect with it) or 4410 (mailbox_gone — stop reconnecting). get.description:
Answers `created` / `updated` / `destroyed` message ids for everything that happened since `since`, plus a `newState` to send next time. Ids only: fetch what you need through the ordinary message endpoints.

**The loop.** Call once with no `since` to get a starting `newState`; do your full listing; then poll with `since=<newState>`, or better, subscribe to `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/events` and call this whenever a frame arrives (a `state.changed` frame's `Email` value is itself a valid `since`). Keep calling while `hasMore` is true.

**What maps to what.** A delivery is `created`, and so is a restore from trash. Flag, keyword and label changes are `updated`, as is a message whose conversation was merged into another. An expunge (soft delete to trash) and a purge are both `destroyed` — this feed mirrors the ordinary live listing, so use `?state=expunged` if you present a trash view. The feed errs toward telling you too much: a message may be reported `created` where `updated` would have done, which costs one refetch. It never reports a message you still hold as `destroyed`.

**When the token is too old** (or was minted by a mailbox that has since been rebuilt) you get `410 cannot_calculate_changes`. There is no repair: re-list the mailbox and bootstrap a fresh token. History is kept for 30 days, comfortably longer than the 14-day trash window, so this only happens to a client that has been away a long time.

post.description:
Send only what the user actually typed. The server derives the rest from the thread: the answerable address (Reply-To before From, and the *recipient* when the newest member is your own Sent copy), the `Subject`, `In-Reply-To`, and a trimmed `References` chain.

Prefer this over `POST /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/send` whenever a reply is what you mean. Broken threading is the classic mail-client bug — every client that rebuilds these headers gets them subtly wrong — so the derivation lives here, in one place. A thread with no answerable address is refused (`400 no_reply_target`) rather than sent to nobody.

The response is the same per-recipient `SendResult` as `/send`, with the same `200` versus `207` rule and the same `X-Delivery-Id` idempotency.

patch.description: Stamps `reportedAt` on one day's row for each named account. Only closed days are stamped; open ones and accounts with no row come back under `skipped` with a reason, and a ledger that could not be reached comes back `unreachable` (retry it). Replays converge — the first stamp is kept, never moved. Stamp FIRST, then export the stamped rows: a closed day can still be corrected by an operator's re-roll until it is stamped, and once stamped nothing rewrites it.
